finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token to the supplied token with loose `==`. PHP type juggling makes two numeric-looking strings equal if they have the same numeric value. For example, stored "0e123..." equals supplied "0" or "0e1". On PHP < 8, a stored string that starts with letters equals integer 0. An attacker can therefore reset the password for any victim whose token has this shape, without knowing the token. The function also uses a non-constant-time comparison.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled $email and $token arguments (for example from a reset form or API), with a victim who has a pending reset row.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... at reset.php:5-6 (account password takeover).

trace.note: The stored token is fetched by the attacker-chosen email.
`$row['token'] == $token` uses loose comparison, so "0e.." == "0e.." or "0" evaluates true.
The victim's password hash is overwritten with the attacker's chosen $new.

finding.guards_checked: No type cast of $token, no strict `===` and no hash_equals. No expiry check and no rate limiting in this file. The sibling reset_password() at line 14 uses hash_equals with a (string) cast and is safe from juggling. I found no callers in the directory, so whether the loose variant is reachable depends on external code. SQL values are escaped with $db->quote(), so I found no SQL injection.

verdict.guard_found: none (only $db->quote() SQL escaping, which doesn't affect the comparison; safe sibling reset_password() at line 14 is not the function in question)
verdict.reason: reset.php:4 compares `$row['token'] == $token` loosely with no cast, hash_equals, expiry or rate limit, so an anonymous caller supplying "0" or "0e1" (or int 0 on PHP<8) can reach the password overwrite at reset.php:5-6, though exploitability depends on the stored token being "0e<digits>" shaped (or PHP<8) and on the unseen callers.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none (the SQL values are escaped with $db->quote(), which blocks injection but not the comparison flaw; the safe hash_equals variant at reset.php:14 is a separate function)
verdict_facts.reason: reset.php:4 uses loose `==` on the stored and supplied tokens with no cast, no hash_equals, and no other check before the password UPDATE at reset.php:5-6, so an anonymous caller can reset a password through type juggling. Exploitation needs a magic-hash stored token ("0e<digits>"), or a non-string $token such as JSON `true` or `0` reaching the function, and random tokens rarely have that shape.

finding.claim: Neither reset function expires the token or deletes the resets row after a successful reset. A token that has leaked, or that was never used, stays valid indefinitely and can be replayed to change the password again. The SELECT also checks no creation time or expiry.
finding.source: An attacker who has obtained an old or leaked reset token for an email (from email logs, a referrer, or a mailbox compromise). Attacker-supplied $email, $token and $new.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... at reset.php:15-16 (repeatable password overwrite).

trace.note: The token row is selected by email with no expiry or timestamp condition.
The token is verified, but no one-time-use or expiry logic follows.
The password is updated and the function returns true without DELETE or invalidating the resets row.

finding.guards_checked: Checked for a DELETE on the resets table, an expiry column, and an attempt counter. None exist in this file. Token generation and storage are outside this directory, so expiry could be enforced elsewhere. hash_equals is used correctly.

verdict.guard_found: none (only hash_equals token comparison at reset.php:14; no expiry, DELETE, or timestamp check anywhere in the directory)
verdict.reason: reset.php:13-17 selects the token by email with no timestamp or expiry condition, and after the hash_equals check at line 14 it updates the password and returns true without deleting or invalidating the resets row, so a leaked or unused token can be replayed; the token's lifecycle outside this directory is unseen, so expiry elsewhere remains possible.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none. Only a token comparison with hash_equals (reset.php:14). There is no DELETE, expiry or timestamp check, and no attempt counter.
verdict_facts.reason: reset.php:13-17 selects the token by email with no time condition, then updates the password and returns true without deleting or invalidating the resets row. An anonymous caller holding a leaked or unused token can therefore replay it. Token generation and any cleanup job live outside this directory, so expiry elsewhere can't be ruled out, but single-use is not enforced here.
